Route briefing · Stage 21 · Dzienniki Rowerowe / Diarios de bicicleta

Medellín → Cartagena

Cześć, Michał!
For Leszek Fidelus and the eleven riders of the final stage 1–16 November 2026 Data checked on 18 October 2026 By Ride The Andes · Duitama, Boyacá
Your question: Ruta 25 north, or Guatapé and the Ruta 45?

Of the two, go east: Guatapé, then the Magdalena.

  • Our pick of your two options: Guatapé, then north on the Ruta 45 (route B).Guatapé is the best stop of the whole stage. From there the Autopista drops about 1,900 m through the Río Claro canyon to the river, so most of your mountain riding next to trucks is downhill. In the valley the Ruta 45 is flat and paved, and OpenStreetMap maps — of route B as divided highway, against — of Ruta 25. At 75 km a day, with a rest day in Mompox, you reach Cartagena on Monday 16 November.
  • Your worry about Ruta 25 is fair.It is the shortest way north (660 km), but the first two days climb from Medellín to Santa Rosa de Osos (2,550 m) on a narrow two-lane road that carries most of the trucks to the coast. With heavy panniers that is the slowest stretch, and the one closest to the trucks, of any option.
  • The heat is the same on both. The Magdalena just has more of it.Caucasia and Sahagún on Ruta 25 are as hot as Puerto Berrío or Aguachica on the Ruta 45: 32–33 °C average November maximum at IDEAM stations. Route B spends about — below 500 m, Ruta 25 about —. Start at first light, around 5:30, and be in town by 13:00: on the flat, 80–90 km fit in that window.
  • Boring? Break it up.Skip the part of your Mapy line between San Carlos and Puerto Nare (more than half of it is dirt or gravel) and take the Autopista through El Santuario, Cocorná and Río Claro. Further north, Mompox is the best rest day of the trip, and the Montes de María and San Basilio de Palenque come just before Cartagena.
  • A dry November.Colombia's weather service (IDEAM) declared El Niño on 8 October 2026 and expects less rain than normal in October and November. The Magdalena is running low. The flood warnings you read come from La Niña years (2010–11, 2020–22); local showers are still possible in the mountains.
  • Prudence, not fear.Ride early and only in daylight, keep your live location to family and friends, post places after you have left them, and ask at the hotel each evening about the next day's road. In a couple of days we will send you how these roads are right now, from riders who live along them.
  • Another option: Guatapé, then Ruta 25 north (route F).If you would rather have mountains than more days of flat heat: after Guatapé, ride back through Marinilla and Guarne, then north on Ruta 25 through the cool dairy highlands of Santa Rosa de Osos and Yarumal, across the Sabanas of Córdoba and Sucre, to Mompox, the Montes de María and Palenque. About 1,030 km, all by bike. It does include the Ruta 25 climb you are worried about, so ride it at first light.
  • Boyacá, our home, is the safest department in the Colombian Andes, but it is too far for this stage. Why, and an invitation for next time.

Po polsku, w skrócie

  • Z Waszych dwóch opcji wybralibyśmy wschód: Guatapé, potem w dół do Magdaleny i Ruta 45 na północ (trasa B). Za Guatapé autostrada opada ok. 1900 m kanionem Río Claro, więc większość jazdy w górach obok ciężarówek to zjazd. W dolinie droga jest płaska i ma długie odcinki dwujezdniowe.
  • Ruta 25: najkrótsza, ale pierwsze dwa dni to podjazd z Medellín do Santa Rosa de Osos wąską drogą, którą jedzie większość ciężarówek na wybrzeże.
  • Upał jest podobny na obu trasach (32–33 °C w listopadzie), w dolinie Magdaleny jest go po prostu więcej dni. Startujcie o świcie (ok. 5:30) i kończcie do 13:00.
  • Żeby nie było nudno: omińcie szutrowy odcinek San Carlos–Puerto Nare z Mapy.com i jedźcie autostradą przez Río Claro. Mompox to najlepsze miejsce na dzień odpoczynku.
  • Ostrożność, bez paniki: jeździjcie wcześnie i tylko za dnia, lokalizację na żywo pokazujcie tylko rodzinie, miejsca publikujcie po wyjeździe. Za kilka dni prześlemy Wam aktualny stan dróg od kolarzy, którzy tam mieszkają.
  • Inna opcja (F): Guatapé, potem Ruta 25 na północ przez Santa Rosa de Osos i Yarumal, Sabany, Mompox, Montes de María i Palenque. Ok. 1030 km, całość na rowerze, ale z podjazdem na Ruta 25.
  • Boyacá, nasz region, to najbezpieczniejszy departament kolumbijskich Andów, ale objazd jest za duży na ten etap. Jeśli kiedyś tam traficie, zapraszamy do naszego sklepu w Duitamie.

Tłumaczenie robocze. Szczegóły i źródła poniżej, po angielsku.

    Side by side

    How the six routes compare

    Distances and climbing come from OpenStreetMap roads routed for a loaded bike. Flood figures are kilometres of road that pass through areas IDEAM mapped as flooded. Days use the pace you set above.

    Advisories: Poland's MSZ (last version we could open: 6 March 2026; the live Odyseusz page was down on 18 October) and the UK FCDO (updated 15 October 2026). The FCDO also names the “southern parts” of Bolívar and Córdoba without drawing a line; Planeta Rica, Sahagún, Magangué and Mompox are in the centre and north of those departments.

    You asked what is absolutely necessary

    Prudence, not fear: what we would not skip

    Ride early, and only in daylight. On the road at first light, around 5:30, and in town by early afternoon. Sunset is around 17:40. The first hours are the coolest of the day, and arriving early leaves time to find the hotel, lock the bikes and ask about tomorrow. In your hot, flat stages in Argentina your tracker shows dawn starts, so you know the drill.
    1. Keep your location to yourselves while you ride.Your Garmin MapShare page is public. For this stage, share it with family and a few trusted people, and post places on Instagram after you have left them, not while you are there.
    2. Ask about tomorrow's road every evening.The hotel owner, the police station, drivers at the fuel station. If a road is closed or a strike is announced, wait a day in town. In a couple of days we will also send you how these roads are right now, from riders who live along them. Road status: Invías on #767 and @SomosInvias.
    3. Sleep in hotels, and book them ahead.No camping and no improvised lodging on this stage. Every night of the planner above ends in a town with hotels. With eleven people, book one or two nights ahead and ask for a room or a garage to lock the bikes inside.
    4. Ride as two or three groups on the highways.Colombian law (Ley 1811 of 2016) lets a group use a full lane and requires drivers to pass at 1.5 m. With trucks, groups of 3–4 with gaps between them are easier to overtake than a line of eleven. Mirrors and rear lights on, also by day.
    1. Túnel de Oriente is closed to bikes.Leave Medellín for Guatapé by Las Palmas or Santa Elena, or by the Autopista. You start on a holiday weekend (Monday 2 November), so expect heavy return traffic on the 2nd.
    2. Carry less, split the rest.Cash in two or three places, passport copies on your phone, and a local SIM (Claro usually has the best rural coverage).
    3. Check your insurance wording once.Poland's MSZ asks travellers to avoid non-essential trips to Magdalena Medio, the middle part of the Ruta 45, and to Urabá. Ask your insurer whether that changes your cover, and register the trip in Odyseusz.
    4. Cartagena will be in fiesta.Independence parade on Thursday 12 November, a holiday on Monday 16 November and hotels close to full. Book the last nights now.
    Using the flood maps properly

    Where the water has been, and why this November is different

    We crossed each route with four IDEAM flood layers: areas flooded during La Niña 2010–11 and 2020–22, zones flooded periodically (2022 map) and the 2001 baseline. The table shows how many kilometres of each route pass through those polygons. The Depresión Momposina (El Banco, Mompox, Magangué) and the lower Cauca (Caucasia) are the classic problem areas. Route B runs — through land that was under water in 2010–11; Ruta 25 (route D), —. In a La Niña year we would tell you to avoid the river towns in November.

    This is not a La Niña year. NOAA puts an 83% chance on a historically strong El Niño from October to December, and IDEAM forecasts below-normal rain for October and November. A dry year can still bring a cloudburst, a flash flood on a side river, or a landslide in the mountain sections: the Autopista near Cocorná was closed for 14 hours this year. Mountains (days 1–3) are where rain matters most for you.

    1–16 November, 25 years of data

    Heat matters more than rain in the lowlands

    From 900 m down, the afternoon feels like 34–37 °C on every route. What changes is how many days of it you ride: route B spends about — below 500 m, Ruta 25 about — and route F about —. The rain figures are typical years; this year should be drier.

    Temperatures and the first rain column: ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo, 1–16 November 2001–2025. “Feels like” is the mean daily maximum apparent temperature. Last column: days with at least 1 mm of rain in November at the nearest IDEAM station, 1991–2020 normals. ERA5 counts light rain generously in the tropics, so trust the station column for how often it rains.

    What your own tracker says

    Your plan asks for twice your usual daily distance

    Your relay has covered about 1,000 km per stage in about 22 days, close to 50 km per calendar day including rest and transfers. Your Mapy plan for stage 21 is 1,217 km. Drawn with Mapy's walking profile, it follows footpaths in places; on roads a loaded bike can use, the same waypoints give 1,101 km and 7,632 m of climbing.

    Your project calendar ends the stage on 22 November, which matches your usual pace. If you have to finish on 12–16 November, the same plan needs 76–101 km every calendar day, in 35 °C heat, with no room for a puncture day. Route B is a little shorter than your Mapy line: at 75 km a day, with a rest day in Mompox, the planner above gets you to Cartagena on Monday 16 November. If you want more slack, that is the one strong argument for Ruta 25: it is about 400 km shorter.

    Source: your public Garmin MapShare feed (3,415 positions, October 2025 to September 2026) and the stage calendar linked from your website. We kept only days with a position at least every hour and no bus-like speeds: 129 riding days.

    About Boyacá, our home

    The safest department in the Colombian Andes, and too far for this stage

    Boyacá had 8.2 homicides per 100,000 people in 2024, a third of the national rate (25.3) and the lowest of any Andean department. Only Guainía and Vaupés, two Amazon departments of about 50,000 people each, were lower.

    We checked a detour. Climbing from Puerto Boyacá through Chiquinquirá, Villa de Leyva, Duitama and San Gil to Bucaramanga, then down to the Magdalena again, is 623 km and +14,100 m. The Ruta del Sol covers the same gap in 193 km and +560 m. That is six or seven extra riding days, so it does not fit this stage.

    If you ever come back to Colombia through Boyacá, you are invited to our shop in Duitama. The coffee is on us, and we will show you the climbs Colombian riders grow up on.

    For a reporting relay

    Stories along the way

    Your best posts are about people. These are the places on the way where the story is the town itself.

    Day 1–2 · Guatapé

    Painted plinths and the Rock

    Most houses wear zócalos, painted relief panels that tell who lives there. Next door, about 700 steps up the Rock of El Peñol.

    Mompox · routes B and F

    A river port the river left behind

    UNESCO town since 1995, silver filigree workshops, and the riverfront García Márquez wrote into The General in His Labyrinth. A good rest day.

    San Jacinto · routes B and F

    Gaitas and hammocks

    Home of the Gaiteros de San Jacinto and of the hammock weavers. A region that is coming back after the war years.

    San Basilio de Palenque

    A free town with its own language

    Founded by people who escaped slavery, and still speaking Palenquero. UNESCO Masterpiece of Intangible Heritage (2005). Six kilometres off the main road, on both B and F.

    How we did this

    Methods and sources

    Methods
    • Routes: BRouter on OpenStreetMap, “moped” profile (main roads, no motorway tunnels), between the towns named on each route. Route A follows the waypoints of your Mapy route “ETAP XXI Medellín Cartagena de Indias”. Surface tags in OSM are incomplete in rural Colombia: check unpaved sections locally.
    • Floods: IDEAM ArcGIS services (Amenaza_Ambiental layers 10, 22, 24; Indicadores_Hidricos layer 21), the same layers we use for land-use planning studies in Boyacá. Kilometres = length of each route inside the polygons.
    • Climate: Open-Meteo historical API (ERA5), 1–16 November 2001–2025, at each town, and IDEAM 1991–2020 station normals for November rain days.
    • Overnight towns: every hotel, motel, guesthouse or hostel mapped in OpenStreetMap within 2 km of the route, grouped by town. Many small-town hotels are not mapped (in Paipa, a spa town near us that is full of hotels, OSM shows five), so the counts are a minimum; the day planner only ends days in these towns.
    • Your pace: public Garmin MapShare KML feed and the stage calendar on dziennikirowerowe.pl. Relief: Mapzen terrain tiles. Rivers and borders: Natural Earth.
    • Security: the Polish MSZ and UK FCDO advisories and Colombian press from January 2025 to October 2026. We use them to choose roads and riding hours; the verdicts are our reading, not an official rating.
    • Divided highway: share of each route on main roads that OpenStreetMap maps as one-way carriageways.
